body: The first account poses this as an agreement-management problem and answers with better infrastructure: write it down, define done, reset weekly, lower the cost of attending. My rival posing sits one level up: why does this flat need so much agreement at all? Three adults with rotating shifts and, almost certainly, different ideas about how clean is clean enough, governing shared space by repeated informal consensus, is a high-friction institution. Better minutes of the meetings do not fix the institution, and may not even fix the meetings. Disputes about what an agreement meant survive writing — they migrate to edge cases (does "counters wiped" include behind the kettle?), to exceptions ("I was on nights"), and to enforcement. And someone has to maintain the written system; that person, likely the asker, becomes household manager, a role that reliably curdles into "nag" and gives the avoiding friend one more reason to stay away. On the avoider: reading withdrawal as a rational response to costly conversations is plausible, but the same behavior fits exit from negotiations the friend keeps losing or never consented to. A channel they can edit on their own time is still an invitation to join a process. The safer design principle is not "make participation cheaper" but "make the system work even if they never participate." So the rival proposal: shrink the coordination surface. (1) Ownership, not consensus — split the flat into domains (kitchen, bathroom, floors-and-bins), each owned long-term by one person, judged by outcome within a floor of reasonableness rather than by compliance with a negotiated spec. The owner schedules around their own shifts; nothing needs co-agreeing weekly; the avoider attends nothing. Domains are unequal, so make the initial split a one-time negotiation using turn-picking or credit-bidding, revisited quarterly rather than weekly — a recurring negotiation cost converted into an occasional one. (2) A variant: rotate whole weeks of total responsibility, one person on and two off. Schedule churn becomes a single swap conversation ("take my deadline week, I'll take your exam week") instead of the redistribution of every chore, and total load becomes visible because everyone eventually carries it. (3) If money exists, buy the argument down: a fortnightly cleaner turns infinitely recurring negotiations into one decision about a bill. (4) And what "what should I do" can mean when you cannot ratify a process for three people: act within your own scope. State which chores you will own and which you will stop silently covering, then hold it. Some things will visibly lapse, and the lapse — not a convened meeting — is what reopens negotiation. This is the riskiest move; it fails if you cannot tolerate undone chores longer than your friends can. The two accounts converge more than they compete. I keep from the visible body: raise the pattern, not the incident, at a calm moment; and its closing warning that refusal across all channels changes the question from chores to the viability of the arrangement. There is even a cheap way to find out which account is right: keep a one-line written note of the next two weeks' agreements — a minimal version of the first account's remedy, run as a diagnostic rather than a fix. If the arguments vanish, recall was the problem and its fuller system is worth building. If they persist in mutated form — fights over what counts, exceptions, tone — the cause is interest or standards, and ownership or decoupling is the better bet. What the material cannot tell either of us: how large the standards gap is, whether any budget exists, how much goodwill remains, and whether the asker is willing to be anyone's manager — which the infrastructure answer quietly requires.
